extracted.intended_audience: women readers seeking guidance on conduct, social etiquette, and personal improvement (19th-century domestic/social context)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for women's everyday conduct and social interactions, covering patience, tact, temper control, dealing with fools, praise versus bluntness, and marriage expectations. Focuses on moral/self-improvement and practical etiquette in family and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be proud of personal defects or peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal defects and eccentricities are 'subjects for regret, not pride.' Boasting of faults (e.g., 'I know I am often impatient, but I simply cannot help it') acknowledges a weakness one should be ashamed of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If undisciplined or untrained in self-control, avoid making others uncomfortable; rather withdraw until you learn self-control. Treat eccentricities as faults to correct, not virtues to celebrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep obtrusive faults out of strong view
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to render an inharmonious color less obtrusive is to keep it out of strong light; applied figuratively to personal faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize the visibility of glaring defects (behavioural or personal) rather than advertising them; practical suggestion for social presentation and tempering disagreeable traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insist others conform to your tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to require other people to 'go well together' with us; people can hold contrary views and still be excellent members of society and reputable Christians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept differences caused by character, environment and education; recognize that someone uncongenial to you might be attractive in their proper surroundings. Avoid demanding others act as 'backgrounds' to your life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give people the justice of seeing their good traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you do not like everybody, do others the justice of seeing their good traits as well as the bad; often seeming uninteresting acquaintances are so because we don't take the trouble to find out what is in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make an effort to discover positive qualities in others before dismissing them; avoid snap judgments based solely on first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a selfish standpoint that breeds boredom
rubrics_metrics.description: People who are always bored may look at everything from 'How does that affect me?' — a selfish standpoint that makes one a bore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether your weariness stems from the other person not talking about topics that interest you; be willing to engage with others' interests and allow conversation to turn to the other person's occupations and likes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the best of everybody (practical/political advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a selfish and politic standpoint it is in our interest to make the best of everybody; we cannot always pick our associates and should secure friendly feeling by looking on their pleasant side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate agreeableness to ensure goodwill; avoid creating unnecessary enemies over small matters since ill-will causes lasting harm and heartache.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privately avoid those you find viscerally repulsive
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a strong, uncontrollable personal antipathy (a 'Dr. Fell'), it is acceptable to avoid that person, but you need not publicize your aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are generally charitable, accept that some visceral repulsion is natural; deal with it discreetly and without broadcasting your dislike to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze causes of dislike; check wounded self-esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudices and dislikes often stem from slight to ourselves or wounded self-esteem; analyze the roots of our feelings of dislike as they may be trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quench sparks of resentment early; don't let small slights ignite long-standing enmity. Reflect honestly to avoid making enemies for transient reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice patience: 'bide a wee' before acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Before taking hasty action (especially angry responses), 'bide a wee' — wait, cool down, and reserve judgment; do not send angry or splenetic letters in the heat of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tempted to reply angrily, tear up or set aside the composition and revisit in the morning. Let excitement cool overnight; this prevents complicating matters and avoids acting 'in the wrong.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior character and evidence before condemning
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging others, take into account established reputation and past proofs of behavior; a single equivocal circumstance should not outweigh years of evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being swayed by half-heard words, misunderstood gestures, or inferior tale-bearers; follow the 'conscientious and impartial trial' principle before assuming a friend false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow others to be mistaken; don't force the truth upon them
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest task is allowing others to know less than we do. Attempting to force the truth on those mistaken often causes dispute, wasted effort, and alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstain from contradicting inessential points; recognize that some differences (dates, opinions) are not worth the quarrel. Let ignorance have its work in many cases rather than incite contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't waste effort arguing with self-conceited fools
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-conceit is the rankest form of folly; arguing with someone who is wise in their own conceit (a self-satisfied blockhead) is like thumping fists against a stone wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize types of folly (stolid stupidity, self-satisfied ignorance) and avoid expending time or temper trying to convert them; use humility as first antidote to folly, and practice restraint when faced with such persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply different conversational rules with fools; sometimes 'let alone' is best
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy and politeness suggest meeting foolish intellects on ground that does not provoke them; to attempt the same standards of debate used with equals is absurd and disagreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let fools 'vapor' if replying only strengthens their belief; sometimes neglecting contradiction will lead them to 'foam out of their own shame.' Be a prudent economist of time and labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be economical with temper and time; avoid losing patience
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing temper does physical and moral harm; the tart speech 'takes virtue out of us.' It is often better to perform the task yourself than to scold (e.g., fatigue yourself by righting an untidy chamber rather than scolding a servant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train in everyday self-control; curb impulses to irritation, especially over domestic service or minor annoyances, to preserve health and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer kind, encouraging words over rough bluntness
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy that a rough tongue is an honest one is pernicious; blunt criticism can be corrosive and damaging, while kind words often heal and encourage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be a healer rather than a 'scarifier.' 'Faithful may be the wounds of a friend' but so are his healings; cultivate the habit of speaking truth 'in love' rather than harsh reproof, avoiding needless cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disagreeable frankness when it harms another's comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not one's duty to be disagreeably frank if another's comfort is the price; an unkind sentence lodges and festers in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from unnecessary unkind remarks (examples: comparing a cottage to a 'charcoal-burner's hut'); speak truth gently and avoid statements that needlessly wound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate gratitude and small acts of courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Small expressions of thanks or appreciation (thanking a policeman, praising a biscuit) can brighten someone's day and have outsized positive effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never neglect to acknowledge small favors; habitual gratitude produces goodwill and can temper otherwise stern dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous with pleasant words ('butter parsnips') but avoid insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair words can make difficult 'parsnips' palatable; kindness and agreeable 'sauce' are preferable to acid criticism. Flattery is not always the only form of kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to be lavishly generous with sincere praise and courtesy ('drown neglected parsnips in fresh butter'), while avoiding obvious hypocrisy; cultivate 'sauce agreable' — pleasant encouragement that aids others' comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage does not reform people; require patience, love, tact
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage has trials and doesn't change fundamental character. After the wedding, each partner returns to their habitual qualities; happiness depends on patience, ample love, and woman's gift of tact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospective spouses should not expect transformation in the other; instead, blend love with patience and tact to live together peacefully, and understand differences in how affection is expressed by lover vs. husband.
